reply.title: Why does a sigmoid squash any number into 0 to 1?
reply.story:
When modeling probabilities or neural activations, we often need to take any real number, from negative infinity to positive infinity, and convert it into a neat score between zero and one. A linear scale fails because it keeps growing without bounds, but a sigmoid curve bends gracefully to form an 'S' shape. As the input climbs higher, the exponential term in the denominator dominates, forcing the output to level off precisely at one. Conversely, large negative inputs drive the denominator to infinity, pushing the output down toward zero.

The steepness parameter controls how rapidly the curve transitions from the lower plateau to the upper one, acting like a magnification glass around the center. Meanwhile, shifting the midpoint moves this central threshold left or right along the axis. Together, these controls dictate how decisively the function maps continuous inputs into bounded probabilities.
